doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: How funding changed: A&E, Japan contract and Kickstarter
summary: He contrasts older big-budget funding (A&E, Hamilton, a Japanese contract for the History of Jazz) with Kickstarter for his Parkinson's film.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well getting back to this, it’s almost step one, you get this idea and then you have to find some funding. Now you’ve got to research, right?

Well things have changed. Everything’s changing. Like technology is changing, information is changing, everything is changing. When I first started doing films, first of all budgets were bigger, because the price of entry was much more expensive. You are shooting on a camera that costs about three thousand dollars, if my memory serves me. I was shooting on cameras that cost seventy thousand dollars. Editing was three or four hundred dollars an hour, or you could edit off-line for fifty or seventy dollars an hour. But you have to go back to 1980s prices, which was double that today. And now you can edit on laptops, so everything is changing. Secondly, so therefore, if you could find sponsors, when I started doing the “Women in Jazz” I went to A&E and A&E paid for stuff. They paid for me, they ended up owning the footage, but I got paid for what I did. When I got the idea — no I didn’t get the idea, Leslie Gourse got the idea — but for those who are watching, I did a film on Joe Williams, a documentary on Joe Williams that Monk was very involved in and it actually came to me, but that was paid for by Hamilton College. And when I did the “History of Jazz” series I went to Japan. I spent a week in Japan negotiating a contract with what was then — it was the Japanese back then, they had money, and they were great jazz lovers. And they couldn’t wait to do

something about jazz. It was a big contract. It was like a half a million dollar contract to do a ten episode series on the history of jazz. David Chertok had set that up actually. And I spent a week in Japan with an attorney, sitting at a conference table with the Japanese. That was funny in itself because they had a translator there, and they would say something in Japanese and then translate it, and then we’d talk among ourselves, and then come up with our answer. And they would translate back to me. After a couple of days we realized they knew English as good as we did, but they were listening to what we were saying. But anyway, today like everything else is changing and like even Occupy Wall Street and Arab Spring and all that, that’s breaking down the hierarchy and everything is going more vertical. We’re turning to each other. Kickstarter — you know about Kickstarter?

Well Kickstarter, you look at all the stuff that’s being funded on Kickstarter, that’s people turning to each other for money. And I am doing this film — I need a lot more than what I’ve raised — but I raised eleven thousand dollars on Kickstarter, that helped me do a critical recording session with Sangeeta — the musician with Parkinson’s — and able- bodied musicians that he used to play with — a very critical part of the film. But I’m struggling now. I go to people, I ask people for money. I’ve gotten shameless. I mean what I really want is to have a producer come in and handle this part for me. But that’s hard to find, especially on a film like this that’ll probably not make a lot of money if it even makes its own money back. So I have to ask everyone for money, and do you need a tax write-off?
It’s like Warren was saying about that next step up of being a band leader.
Exactly. Exactly. He never wanted to do it. Exactly.

You know I find I’m happier working with other people and okay, Burrill you do this part and you’ll do that part, rather than where I have to do everything myself. And I’m — hey, look at me, I’m not young anymore. And it gets hard.
